title: Manage Third-Party and AI Supply Chain Risks
intro: How to assess AI providers and their security controls; the procurement controls, security SLAs and incident notification rights that make vendor risk manageable; tracking AI components with SBOMs and AIBOMs; shared responsibility across AI SaaS, model APIs and self-hosting; and data centre security, trusted execution environments and confidential computing.
objectives: Run proportionate due diligence on AI providers, using certifications, AI-specific control frameworks and evidence
Define procurement controls and contract terms: security SLAs, incident notification, model change notice, data use, audit and exit
Align vendor incident notification with GDPR, NIS2 and EU AI Act deadlines
Explain SBOMs and AIBOMs, what an AIBOM records, and how it supports incident response
Apply shared responsibility models to AI SaaS, model APIs and self-hosted models
Assess data centre security for AI and explain TEEs, attestation and the limits of confidential computing

scenes.title: Buying AI safely

scenes.say: Most organisations don’t build their AI. They buy it, as a hosted model, an AI feature inside a SaaS product, or a platform. You can outsource the work, but not the accountability. | This video covers how to assess AI providers, the procurement controls and contract terms that matter, and how incident notification should work.

scenes.title: The AI procurement lifecycle
scenes.say: Procurement is a lifecycle, not a one-off check. It starts with the need, and the use case’s risk tier, which sets how deep the assessment goes. | Due diligence gathers answers and, more importantly, evidence: certificates, audit reports and test results. | The contract turns findings into enforceable commitments: service levels, data terms and notification rights. | Onboarding configures the service securely, with single sign-on, logging, data controls and safety settings switched on. | Monitoring tracks performance, model changes, sub-processor changes and incidents for as long as the service is used. | And exit is planned from day one: data returned, deletion certified, and a transition path to an alternative.

scenes.say: Incident notification terms must fit your legal deadlines. | Under the GDPR, a controller must notify the regulator within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, and processors must tell controllers without undue delay. | Under the NIS2 directive, essential and important entities send an early warning within twenty-four hours, and a fuller notification within seventy-two. | Under the AI Act, serious incidents involving high-risk AI must be reported within fifteen days, or two days for critical infrastructure disruption or widespread infringement. | So the contract must require the vendor to notify you well inside your shortest clock, often within twenty-four hours, or you will miss yours.

blocks.md:
### Why third-party AI needs its own due diligence
Traditional vendor assessments ask about access control, encryption and certifications. AI providers raise additional questions: whether your prompts and data train their models, how they evaluate and red-team their models, how and when models change, where inference happens, which other model providers they depend on, and how their safety systems work. Regulation also assigns roles: under the EU AI Act, an organisation integrating a vendor’s model into its own high-risk product may become a **provider**, inheriting obligations it can only meet with the vendor’s cooperation.

Due diligence should be **proportionate to the use-case tier** (Module 2.3): a tier-1 writing tool needs a short check of data terms; a tier-4 decision system needs a deep review with evidence.

### Sources of assurance
- **Certifications and reports:** ISO/IEC 27001 (information security), **ISO/IEC 42001** (AI management system), SOC 2 Type II reports, and sector certifications. Check scope: a certificate that covers the vendor’s corporate IT but not its AI platform is of little use.
- **CSA AI Controls Matrix (AICM) and STAR for AI:** the Cloud Security Alliance’s AICM is a vendor-neutral set of AI security and governance control objectives (247 across 18 domains in version 1.1), mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act. STAR for AI offers self-assessment (level 1) and third-party certification (level 2).
- **Model and system documentation:** model cards, system cards, evaluation and red-teaming summaries, acceptable use policies, and the provider’s training-data summary where required.
- **Questionnaires:** standardised questionnaires (with AI-specific sections) supplemented by targeted questions and requests for evidence.
- **Testing:** your own evaluation of the service against your use case, including adversarial tests, within the provider’s terms.

### Key due diligence questions
| Area | Questions |
|---|---|
| Data handling | Are prompts, outputs and files retained? For how long? Are they used to train or improve models? Can that be switched off contractually? Where are they processed and stored? Which sub-processors (including other model providers) receive them? |
| Security | How is customer data isolated? How are model weights and infrastructure protected? What logging is available to customers? How are vulnerabilities in the AI stack handled? |
| Model governance | How are models evaluated for safety, bias and security before release? Are red-team results shared? How are model updates announced, and can versions be pinned? |
| Safety systems | What content filtering and abuse monitoring operate, and can they be configured? What data does abuse monitoring retain, and who reviews it? |
| Resilience | What are the uptime commitments, rate limits and capacity guarantees? What happens during an outage? |
| Legal | Who owns outputs? Is there an IP indemnity, and on what conditions? How are liability and regulatory responsibilities allocated? |

### Contract and procurement controls
- **Security SLAs:** availability, latency, support response, and **vulnerability remediation timelines**, with service credits or other remedies.
- **Incident notification rights:** notification within a defined period (often 24 hours or less), minimum content (what happened, data affected, actions taken), ongoing updates, cooperation with investigations and regulators, and access to relevant logs.
- **Change management:** advance notice of model version changes, deprecations and sub-processor changes, with rights to object or exit.
- **Data terms:** no training on customer data, retention limits (zero data retention where needed), data location, encryption and key management options, deletion on termination with **certification**.
- **Audit rights:** access to independent reports, the right to send questionnaires and, for critical services, to audit.
- **Exit and portability:** data export in usable formats, transition assistance, and continued service during migration.
- **Flow-down:** obligations apply to the vendor’s sub-processors.

Regulated sectors face specific requirements. In the EU, **DORA** requires financial entities to maintain a register of ICT third-party arrangements and include defined contractual provisions, and **NIS2** sets incident reporting timelines for essential and important entities. Vendor terms must make your own compliance possible.

### Incident notification clocks
| Regime | Clock |
|---|---|
| GDPR (controller → supervisory authority) | Within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach; processors notify controllers without undue delay |
| NIS2 (essential and important entities) | Early warning within 24 hours; incident notification within 72 hours; final report within one month |
| EU AI Act Article 73 (providers of high-risk AI) | Within 15 days of awareness; within 2 days for widespread infringement or serious critical-infrastructure incidents; within 10 days for a death |

Design vendor notification terms back from your **shortest** applicable clock, leaving time to assess and decide.

blocks.title: The standard terms
blocks.md: A legal team wants to buy an AI contract-review service. The vendor’s standard terms say customer documents may be used “to improve our services”, incidents will be reported “within a reasonable time”, and model versions “may change without notice”. The vendor holds ISO/IEC 27001 certification for its corporate offices only.

q.q: What is the BEST next step?
o: Sign, because the vendor’s ISO/IEC 27001 certification already covers how it handles customer documents
Negotiate no training on customer data, prompt incident notice, notice of model changes and AI platform assurance first
Ask the vendor to confirm in a follow-up email that it won’t use the documents for training, analytics or any other purpose
Use the service only for non-confidential contracts, and leave the standard terms unchanged for now
q.why: Each standard term creates risk: training use breaches confidentiality, vague notification breaks regulatory clocks, and silent model changes undermine testing. The certificate doesn’t cover the AI service. Contractual commitments and relevant assurance must come first.

q.q: An organisation subject to NIS2 relies on an AI vendor for a critical service. What should the vendor contract require for incident notification?
o: Notification within 30 days, matching the vendor’s standard service-level reporting cycle
Notification fast enough to meet the 24-hour early warning duty, with defined content and cooperation
No notification clause, since the vendor is responsible under NIS2 for reporting its own incidents
Notification only when personal data is affected, because NIS2 incident reporting follows the GDPR
q.why: The organisation’s own deadline (24-hour early warning under NIS2) depends on learning of vendor incidents quickly. Contract terms must fit inside that clock and include enough detail to act.

blocks.md:
### Why dependency tracking matters for AI
Supply-chain attacks and vulnerable dependencies are among the most common routes to compromise in software, and AI adds new dependency types. Examples include malicious model files that execute code when loaded (some serialisation formats, such as Python pickle, can run arbitrary code), poisoned public datasets, compromised fine-tuning adapters, vulnerable inference servers, and third-party plugins or MCP servers with excessive permissions. The **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications** lists supply chain (LLM03:2025) as a top risk.

### SBOM and AIBOM
A **software bill of materials (SBOM)** is a formal, machine-readable inventory of software components, versions, suppliers, dependency relationships and licences. Common formats are **SPDX** and **CycloneDX**. An **AI bill of materials (AIBOM)** extends this to AI-specific components:

| AIBOM element | Examples |
|---|---|
| Model identity | Name, version, supplier, format, **cryptographic hash or signature** |
| Model lineage | Base model, fine-tuning runs, adapters, training dates, training organisation |
| Datasets | Source and provenance, licence, collection method, sensitivity classification, version, preprocessing |
| Software | Training and inference frameworks, libraries, container images, serving stack (from the SBOM) |
| Services | External model APIs, embedding services, plugins, tools and MCP servers |
| Hardware | Accelerator types and firmware, where relevant to security or reproducibility |
| Licences and restrictions | Permitted uses, attribution, commercial limits, acceptable use policies |
| Evaluation and limitations | Links to model cards, evaluation results, known vulnerabilities and limitations |

**CycloneDX** supports machine-learning BOMs (ML-BOM) with fields for models and datasets, and **SPDX 3.0** introduced **AI** and **Dataset** profiles. Standards and community initiatives (including OWASP work on AIBOMs and US government work on SBOMs for AI) are maturing quickly; the governance requirement is stable: **for every AI system, know which models, datasets and components it uses, where they came from, and under what terms**.

### Using AIBOMs
- **Vulnerability and incident response:** match advisories against AIBOMs to find affected systems.
- **Procurement:** request AIBOMs from suppliers (or the information to build them) as a contract term.
- **Licence compliance:** check that every model and dataset is used within its licence.
- **Change control:** a new model version or dataset produces a new AIBOM version, linked to the inventory record and risk assessment.
- **Integrity:** store hashes and signatures so deployed artefacts can be verified against the AIBOM (Module 3.6 covers signing).

### Shared responsibility models
Cloud providers popularised the **shared responsibility model**: the provider secures some layers, the customer secures the rest. AI adds layers such as model safety, prompts and retrieval data:

| Layer | AI SaaS (e.g., a copilot) | Model API (PaaS) | Self-hosted model on IaaS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Physical data centre, hardware, hypervisor | Provider | Provider | Provider |
| Model hosting, scaling, patching of serving stack | Provider | Provider | **Customer** |
| Base model training and built-in safety | Provider | Provider | Model supplier / **customer** |
| Application, orchestration, plugins | Provider | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Prompts, guardrail configuration, content filters | Shared (customer configures) | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Data (inputs, RAG sources, outputs) | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Identity, access, user behaviour | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |
| Accountability for use, outcomes and compliance | **Customer** | **Customer** | **Customer** |

Three practical lessons:
1. **Read the provider’s responsibility documentation** and map each responsibility to an owner in your organisation; gaps appear where each side assumes the other is responsible.
2. **Configure what you own:** the most common cloud and SaaS failures are customer misconfigurations, such as overly broad data access for a copilot.
3. **Accountability is never transferred**, whatever the contract says about responsibility for specific controls.

blocks.title: AIBOM questions
blocks.md: If a question asks how to **rapidly determine which systems are affected** by a compromised model, dataset or library, the answer is an **AIBOM** (or SBOM for software-only components) linked to the **AI inventory**. If it asks who is responsible for a misconfigured SaaS AI feature, the answer is usually the **customer**, because configuration and data access sit on the customer’s side of the shared responsibility line.

q.q: A public dataset used by many organisations is found to contain poisoned samples. Which capability lets you MOST quickly identify which of your models were trained on it?
o: A firewall rule that blocks downloads from the dataset’s public repository
AI bills of materials recording datasets and lineage for each model, linked to the inventory
An acceptable use policy requiring teams to vet every public dataset before they use it in training
Annual penetration testing of the machine learning platform and its training pipelines
q.why: AIBOMs record which datasets and versions each model used. Querying them, with owners from the inventory, turns the advisory into a targeted response.

scenes.say: Ask six questions about the data centres behind an AI service. | Location and sovereignty: in which countries is data processed, which laws apply there, and can you pin processing to specific regions? | Certification and audits: does their scope actually cover the AI platform and its facilities? | Power, cooling and resilience: AI accelerators run at very high density, so check redundancy and recovery arrangements. | Tenancy and isolation: are GPUs and their memory shared between customers, and how are they isolated and cleared? | Hardware supply chain: how is firmware integrity verified and patched? | And key control: can you manage your own keys, in hardware security modules, and who can decrypt your data?

scenes.title: Three states of data
rows: Host OS, hypervisor, operators, memory scraping
scenes.say: Data exists in three states. | At rest, it is protected by disk and database encryption. In transit, by TLS. In use, it has traditionally been decrypted in memory, where only a trusted execution environment can protect it. | Encryption at rest defends against stolen media and backups, and TLS against interception. But while a model processes a prompt, the data and the model weights sit in memory, exposed to the host operating system, the hypervisor, and anyone who controls them, including the cloud operator. Confidential computing closes that gap.

scenes.title: How confidential inference works

nodes.label: Key broker
nodes.sub: releases keys only to attested TEEs

nodes.label: TEE: CPU and GPU
nodes.sub: model and prompt decrypted only inside

note.text: The operator runs the hardware but can’t read the data or the weights.

scenes.say: Here is confidential inference in outline. A client wants to send a sensitive prompt to a model running in a cloud. | First it checks an attestation: a signed report, produced by the hardware itself, proving that the workload runs on genuine trusted hardware, with exactly the expected code and configuration. | Only if the attestation checks out does the client send its encrypted request. Inside the trusted execution environment, which can now span both the CPU and the GPU, the prompt and the model are decrypted and processed. | A key broker releases decryption keys, including those for the model weights, only to environments that pass attestation. | So the operator runs the hardware, but can’t read the prompts, the outputs or the weights.

scenes.title: Trusted execution technologies

items.d: Protect part of an application, such as Intel SGX
Protect a whole virtual machine: Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP
Arm Confidential Compute Architecture
Protected GPU memory and CPU–GPU transfers, on recent data-centre GPUs

scenes.say: Several technologies provide trusted execution. | Process enclaves protect part of an application. Intel SGX is the best-known example. | Confidential virtual machines protect an entire virtual machine from the hypervisor. Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP work this way. | Arm’s Confidential Compute Architecture provides protected realms. | And recent data-centre GPUs add confidential computing modes that protect GPU memory and the data moving between the CPU and the GPU, which is what makes confidential AI practical.

scenes.title: What confidential computing doesn’t fix

items.d: Researchers have repeatedly found ways to leak data from TEEs
Firmware, attestation keys and patches still matter
An unverified report proves nothing
Prompt injection works just as well inside an enclave

scenes.say: Confidential computing is powerful, but it has limits. | Side channels: researchers have repeatedly found ways to leak data from trusted environments, so patching and hardening remain essential. | You still trust the hardware vendor’s firmware, attestation keys and update process. | Attestation must actually be verified against expected values. A report nobody checks proves nothing. | And it doesn’t fix application flaws. A prompt injection attack, or a model that leaks data in its answers, works just as well inside an enclave.

items: Check location, certification scope, resilience, isolation, firmware, keys
Protect data at rest, in transit and in use
TEEs plus attestation keep data and weights from the operator
Side channels, vendor trust and app flaws remain
scenes.say: To recap. | When assessing data centres behind AI services, check location, certification scope, resilience, tenant isolation, hardware supply chain and key control. | Protect data in all three states: at rest, in transit and in use. | Trusted execution environments, with verified attestation and attested key release, can keep prompts and model weights hidden even from the operator. | But side channels, trust in the hardware vendor and application-level flaws still need managing.

blocks.md:
### Data centre security considerations for AI
When AI runs in third-party facilities (a hyperscaler, a GPU cloud, a colocation site or a model provider’s own infrastructure), the organisation inherits that facility’s risks. Key considerations:

| Consideration | What to check |
|---|---|
| **Location and sovereignty** | Countries and regions of processing and storage; ability to restrict regions; government access laws; transfer mechanisms for personal data |
| **Certification scope** | ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 and sector certifications that explicitly cover the AI platform and the facilities it runs in |
| **Physical and environmental** | Access control, surveillance, power and cooling redundancy (AI racks draw far more power than traditional servers), fire suppression; Module 4.2 covers these in depth |
| **Tenancy and isolation** | Whether accelerators are shared between customers; memory clearing between jobs; isolation of training and inference workloads |
| **Hardware and firmware supply chain** | Trusted sourcing, firmware signing and verification, patch processes for drivers and accelerator firmware |
| **Key management** | Customer-managed keys (BYOK), hold-your-own-key models, hardware security modules, and who can access keys |
| **Resilience** | Capacity guarantees, multi-region failover, recovery objectives for AI services |

### Confidential computing
The Confidential Computing Consortium defines confidential computing as **the protection of data in use by performing computation in a hardware-based, attested trusted execution environment (TEE)**. A TEE isolates code and data in memory so that the host operating system, hypervisor, other tenants and the infrastructure operator can’t read or alter them.

**Remote attestation** is what makes TEEs useful across organisations: the hardware produces a signed measurement of the code and configuration running in the TEE, which a relying party verifies before trusting it with data or keys. A **key broker** (or key release policy) releases secrets, such as model decryption keys or data keys, only to TEEs whose attestation matches an expected policy.

| Technology | Scope |
|---|---|
| Intel SGX | Application enclaves protecting part of a process |
| Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP | Confidential virtual machines protecting an entire VM from the hypervisor |
| Arm CCA | “Realms” isolated from the normal and secure worlds |
| Confidential GPU computing | Protected GPU memory and encrypted CPU–GPU transfers on recent data-centre GPUs, so AI workloads can run inside a TEE spanning CPU and GPU |

### AI use cases
- **Protecting model weights** deployed on infrastructure you don’t control, for example a model provider deploying into a customer’s cloud, or an organisation running a proprietary model on a GPU cloud.
- **Protecting prompts and data** from the model provider and cloud operator, for regulated or highly confidential processing. Some providers now offer inference in attested environments with published, verifiable software images.
- **Multi-party collaboration:** training or evaluating on combined datasets from several organisations, where none should see the others’ raw data (often combined with federated learning or data clean rooms).

### Limitations
- **Side-channel attacks** against TEEs have been demonstrated repeatedly; keep firmware and microcode patched and follow vendor guidance.
- **Trust shifts to the hardware vendor** and its attestation infrastructure.
- **Attestation is only as good as its verification:** relying parties must check measurements against expected values and policies, and update them as software changes.
- **Performance overhead** and operational complexity are real, though shrinking.
- **TEEs don’t fix application-layer risks:** prompt injection, insecure output handling, excessive agency and model leakage of training data still need their own controls.

blocks.title: Confidential computing vocabulary
cards: A hardware-isolated area where code and data are protected from the host, hypervisor and operator.
Protecting data in use by computing inside a hardware-based, attested TEE.
A hardware-signed proof of what code and configuration run inside a TEE, verified by a relying party.
A service that releases secrets only to TEEs whose attestation matches policy.
A virtual machine whose memory is encrypted and isolated from the hypervisor (for example, TDX or SEV-SNP).
Bring your own key (customer-managed keys in the provider’s KMS) / hold your own key (keys stay outside the provider).

blocks.title: The proprietary model in a GPU cloud
blocks.md: A firm has trained a proprietary fraud model that is a key competitive asset. It needs to run inference on a third-party GPU cloud for capacity reasons, and worries about the cloud operator or other tenants accessing the weights.

q.q: Which approach BEST protects the model weights while in use?
o: Encrypt the weights at rest in object storage, and restrict the storage bucket to the inference service
Run inference in confidential VMs with GPU TEEs, releasing the decryption key only after attestation
Obfuscate and rename the model files on the provider’s hosts, so they are hard to find and copy
Rely on the provider’s non-disclosure agreement and its contractual liability for any misuse of the weights
q.why: Encryption at rest doesn’t protect weights once loaded into memory. Confidential computing with attested key release keeps weights encrypted outside the TEE and readable only inside verified environments. Contracts help but don’t technically prevent access.

q.q: A team proposes moving its LLM application into a TEE to stop prompt injection attacks. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree; TEEs isolate the application, so injected instructions can’t reach the model at runtime
Explain that TEEs protect against the host and operator, not application-layer attacks like prompt injection
Agree, provided remote attestation is enabled so only verified prompts can enter the enclave
Disagree, because TEEs can’t run AI workloads on GPUs, so the application would have to move to CPU-only servers
q.why: Confidential computing addresses infrastructure-level threats to data in use. Prompt injection exploits the application’s logic and works the same way inside a TEE.

quiz.q: A vendor’s ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers only its corporate offices. What does this mean for an assessment of its AI platform?
o: The platform is fully assured, because ISO/IEC 27001 certification applies to the whole company
It offers little assurance for the AI platform, so further evidence covering the platform is needed
Certificates never matter in AI assessments, because AI platforms change too quickly to certify
The vendor must be rejected immediately, because a partial scope means the certificate is invalid
quiz.why: Certification scope matters. Assurance must cover the systems and facilities that actually deliver the AI service.

quiz.q: Which framework provides vendor-neutral AI security and governance control objectives, mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act?
o: PCI DSS v4.0.1
The CSA AI Controls Matrix
ITIL 4 for AI services
COBIT 2019 with AI extensions
quiz.why: The Cloud Security Alliance’s AI Controls Matrix (AICM) underpins its STAR for AI programme and maps to major AI frameworks.

quiz.q: Why should an AI vendor contract require advance notice of model version changes?
o: To reduce licence costs, because older model versions are priced lower
Silent model updates can change behaviour, including safety, and invalidate your testing
Because each new model version changes the vendor’s tax position in the different countries it operates in
It is a GDPR requirement for all software that processes personal data in the EU
quiz.why: Notice, plus the ability to pin versions, lets you re-test before a changed model reaches your users.

quiz.q: Under NIS2, how quickly must an essential or important entity send an early warning of a significant incident?
o: Within 24 hours
Within 7 days
Within 30 days
There is no deadline
quiz.why: NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within one month. Vendor terms must fit inside these clocks.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what is the general deadline for providers to report a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system?
o: 72 hours
15 days
30 days
6 months
quiz.why: Article 73 sets 15 days generally, with shorter limits of 2 days for widespread infringement or critical-infrastructure incidents and 10 days for a death.

quiz.q: What does an AIBOM add to a traditional SBOM?
o: Nothing; an AIBOM is simply an SBOM generated by an AI tool rather than by hand
Models, datasets, adapters, training lineage and related licences, alongside software
Only the hardware serial numbers of the GPUs and servers used to train each model
Only the vendor’s performance claims, such as benchmark scores, for each model version
quiz.why: An AIBOM extends software inventories to AI-specific components and their provenance, which incident response and licence compliance depend on.

quiz.q: Which formats support machine-readable AI or ML bills of materials?
o: CSV and XLSX spreadsheets with a standard column layout
CycloneDX (ML-BOM) and SPDX 3.0 (AI and Dataset profiles)
OpenAPI 3.1 and JSON Schema for model interfaces
PDF/A documents that are digitally signed by the model’s publisher
quiz.why: Both major SBOM standards have extended to AI: CycloneDX with ML-BOM and SPDX 3.0 with AI and Dataset profiles.

quiz.q: An organisation uses a SaaS copilot that can read too many internal document libraries. Under the shared responsibility model, who is primarily responsible for fixing this?
o: The SaaS provider, because it built the copilot and controls the AI model
The customer, because data access configuration is on the customer’s side
The cloud data centre operator that hosts the SaaS provider’s infrastructure
The model developer, because the copilot’s retrieval behaviour comes from training
quiz.why: In SaaS, customers own their data, identities and configuration, including which content the copilot may access.

quiz.q: What does remote attestation provide in confidential computing?
o: Faster processing of encrypted data, because the TEE decrypts it in hardware
A hardware-signed proof of what code and configuration are running in a TEE, verified before trust
Automatic encryption of every backup and snapshot taken from the confidential virtual machine at rest
A secure copy of the model weights that the relying party can inspect before sending data
quiz.why: Attestation lets a client or key broker verify the environment before releasing data or keys to it.

quiz.q: Which threat does confidential computing NOT address?
o: A cloud operator reading data in memory
A malicious hypervisor
Prompt injection against the application
Another tenant reading GPU memory
quiz.why: TEEs protect data and code from the infrastructure layer. Application-layer attacks such as prompt injection work the same inside a TEE.

exam.q: A business unit wants to adopt an AI meeting-transcription service for board meetings. Which due diligence question is MOST important?
o: How accurate are its transcripts for board members with different accents and speaking styles?
Are transcripts retained or used for training, where are they processed, and by which sub-processors?
How many languages does it support, and can it translate transcripts for overseas board members?
Does it integrate with the company’s calendar and board portal so meetings are recorded automatically?
exam.why: Board discussions are highly confidential. Data retention, training use, location and sub-processors determine the confidentiality risk; features are secondary.

exam.q: A vendor will notify incidents “within a reasonable time”. The organisation is subject to GDPR and NIS2. What is the BEST contractual change?
o: Accept the term, since vendors act in good faith and “reasonable” is a well-understood legal standard
Require notice within the shortest regulatory clock (for example, 24 hours), with set content and cooperation
Require monthly incident summaries, which give the organisation a complete picture of the vendor’s incidents
Replace the clause with a right to audit the vendor annually, which covers incident handling more fully
exam.why: Vague notification can make the organisation miss its own deadlines (24-hour NIS2 early warning, 72-hour GDPR notification). A specific, short clock with defined content is needed.

exam.q: An advisory reports that a widely used embedding model contains a backdoor. The CISO asks which production systems use it. The organisation has SBOMs for its applications but no records of models or datasets. What is the BEST long-term improvement?
o: Ask developers to keep a shared spreadsheet of every model and dataset they use, updated at each release cycle
Extend SBOMs into AIBOMs recording models, versions, hashes, datasets and lineage, linked to the inventory
Ban third-party embedding models and require every team to train its own from scratch in future
Ask every AI vendor to email the CISO whenever a security issue affects one of their models
exam.why: SBOMs cover software libraries but not models or datasets. AIBOMs linked to the inventory make this question answerable in minutes.

exam.q: A team builds an application on a hosted model API. A user extracts confidential data from the application’s retrieval index through crafted questions. Under shared responsibility, who must primarily address this?
o: The model API provider, because it hosts the model that generated the confidential answers
The customer, because the app, retrieval data, access controls and filters are on its side
The end user who crafted the questions, who is legally responsible for the extraction
The internet service provider, which should have detected the unusual queries in transit
exam.why: With a model API, the customer owns the application layer, including retrieval data and its permissions, prompts and output filtering. Accountability for outcomes stays with the customer in every model.

exam.q: A bank wants to use a cloud LLM to analyse confidential customer documents, but its regulator is concerned about cloud operator access to data during processing. Which control MOST directly addresses this concern?
o: Encryption at rest with customer-managed keys held in the bank’s own on-premises hardware security modules
Confidential computing with verified attestation, so documents are decrypted only inside TEEs
A longer contract with stronger confidentiality clauses, audit rights and penalties for any operator access
Daily backups of all processed documents to an on-premises location
exam.why: The concern is data in use. Encryption at rest and in transit don’t protect data while it is processed; attested TEEs do.

exam.q: A provider claims its confidential AI service is secure because it runs in TEEs. Which follow-up question is MOST important?
o: Which certifications does the data centre hold, and how often are its physical controls audited?
How is attestation verified, how are TEE flaws patched, and what application-layer controls exist?
How many GPUs does the provider own, and can it guarantee capacity during peak demand periods?
Is the confidential service cheaper than competitors, and does the price include attestation?
exam.why: TEE assurance depends on verified attestation and patched hardware, and TEEs don’t cover application-layer risks. These questions test whether the claim holds.
